The Torah Teaching and Educational-Public Activity of Rabbi Moshe Tzvi Neriah: Architect of the Knitted Kippah Generation

This text surveys the work of Rabbi Moshe Tzvi Neriah, considered the father of the knitted kippah generation, and details how he shaped modern religious-Zionist identity in Israel. The survey traces his roots in the Jewish underground in the Soviet Union and his deep connection to Chabad Hasidism, alongside his becoming a distinguished student of Rabbi Kook who translated his teaching into pioneering educational practice. The crowning achievement of his accomplishments is the establishment of Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh, where the model of the high school yeshiva crystallized, combining sacred studies with general education and active involvement in the state. The article emphasizes his theological conception viewing Israeli sovereignty as "athalta detquva" [the beginning of redemption], and describes his wide-ranging influence through his literary writing, public leadership, and raising a generation of leaders who combine loyalty to halakhah with service for the common good.

The Torah Teaching and Educational-Public Activity of Rabbi Moshe Tzvi Neriah: Architect of the Knitted Kippah Generation

Introduction: The Cultural-Educational Revolution of the Father of the Knitted Kippah Generation

Rabbi Moshe Tzvi Neriah (21 Shevat 5673 – 19 Kislev 5756; January 29, 1913 – December 12, 1995), born Moshe Tzvi Mankin, is considered by scholars and historians to be the spiritual and educational father of the "knitted kippah generation."[1, 2, 3, 4] He functioned as a living and turbulent bridge between the old East European yeshiva world and emerging Israeli society, and led an unprecedented sociological and cultural revolution within Religious Zionism.[2, 4, 5] His central vision was driven by an aspiration to spread Torah study among the young generation in the Land of Israel, based on the foundational assumption that Torah education would produce a moral and qualitative majority that would shape the legal system, culture, and leadership of the young sovereign state.[6]

Rabbi Neriah translated the theological and metaphysical philosophy of his distinguished teacher, Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak HaCohen Kook [the Rayah Kook], into daily educational and social practice.[2, 4, 5] He succeeded in instilling in pioneering youth a proud self-awareness combining absolute loyalty to halakhah with active involvement in building the Land, military service, and practical life.[5, 7] Analysis of his work and Torah teaching reveals a multidimensional figure who united Lithuanian scholarly rootedness, depth and enthusiasm of Chabad Hasidism, and active Zionist nationalism.[4, 8]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Spiritual Development and Life Stations: From the Soviet Underground to Merkaz HaRav

Rabbi Neriah's roots are planted in the town of Łódź in Poland, where he was born to his father, Rabbi Petahiah Mankin, and his mother, Rabbanit Rachel.[3, 4, 9] Due to decrees of the Soviet regime that closed traditional Jewish educational institutions, he was forced to study Torah from his father in his childhood.[3, 9] At only age 13 he exiled himself to a place of Torah and went to study at the Yeshiva of Minsk under the leadership of Rabbi Yehoshua Hordoner, which operated under difficult underground conditions and under constant danger from the Soviet secret police.[4] In Minsk his deep connection to the world of Hasidism began, when he joined a clandestine study group in the "Lubavitcher shtibl" of the city under the tutelage of the mashpia [spiritual mentor] Rabbi Avraham Baruch Pevzner.[4] This group, organized by a student named Lipa, studied for an entire year "Sha'ar HaYihud VeHaEmunah" [The Gate of Unity and Faith], and in the month of Elul "Iggeret HaTeshuvah" [The Epistle on Repentance] together with "Kuntres HaTefillah" [Tract on Prayer] by the Admor HaZaken [the Alter Rebbe], and participated in secret gatherings.[4]

In the years 5680-5689 [1920-1929] Rabbi Neriah moved to Shklov, where he studied under Rabbi Mordechai Feinstein, brother of the posek [halakhic decisor] of the generation Rabbi Moshe Feinstein, until the arrest of the yeshiva students on the night of 23 Shevat 5690 [1930].[4] He fled to Moscow and lived in poverty with his brother, Rabbi Yosef Mankin.[4] In Moscow he met Zisel Bonin and Rabbi David Chanzin, with whom he established a regular havruta [study partnership] in the suburb of Cherkizovo.[4] The two studied Tractate Bava Kama in depth and recited Tractate Pesahim by heart.[4]

To escape from the Soviet Union required the enormous sum of thirty dollars for a passport.[4] Rabbi Neriah appealed to various figures abroad, and ultimately the Admor, the Rayatz [Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak] of Lubavitch, sent him the full amount, which enabled his rescue and his aliyah to the Land of Israel on 23 Sivan 5690 [1930] with the assistance of Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Kook.[4] Upon his arrival in the Land he entered to study at the "Merkaz HaRav" yeshiva in Jerusalem, where he became bound in bonds of love to the Rayah Kook and became his close student.[2, 4, 5] Rabbi Kook even established with him and with Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli a regular havruta to prepare his weekly general lecture.[2] In this yeshiva Rabbi Neriah shaped his national consciousness and his literary name "Neriah," which began as an underground pseudonym in writing articles for Bnei Akiva out of a desire to avoid political controversies, and in time became his official family name.[2, 5]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Establishment of Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh: The "Republic" of Torah Students and the Polemic over Secular Studies

Yeshivat Bnei Akiva at Kfar HaRoeh, founded on 10 Heshvan 5700 [1939], is considered the mother of Bnei Akiva yeshivot and the great experimental laboratory of Religious Zionism.[10] The establishment of the yeshiva arose from the intense demand of the "Torah circles" in Bnei Akiva branches in Jerusalem, Haifa, and Petah Tikva, who desired a pioneering yeshiva where they would study in Hebrew and in the spirit of the movement.[10]

In the summer of 5699 [1939] members of the circles went on a "preparation camp" at Kfar HaRoeh under the direction of Tzvi Kaplan and accompanied by Rabbi Avraham Tzukerman.[10] Rabbi Neriah himself was not present at the camp since he served at that time as a delegate to the 21st Zionist Congress in Geneva.[10] With the outbreak of World War II, fundraising encountered severe difficulties; the president of Mizrachi, Rabbi Meir Bar-Ilan, refused to assist due to war circumstances, while Moshe Haim Shapira provided temporary budget for a trial, and Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon supported the project from his private pocket.[10]

On 10 Heshvan 5700 [1939] the first 13 students arrived under the leadership of Rabbi Neriah at the moshav, settled in the synagogue hut, and began studying Tractate Beitzah.[10, 11] The unique curriculum combined Gemara, Mishnayot of Seder Zera'im, Tanakh, and writings of the Rayah.[10, 11] Rabbi Neriah defined the way of life in the institution as a "republic of Torah students," in which an elected student council managed social life, established regulations, and decided on admission of new students.[10, 11]

In the yeshiva's early years agricultural labor was integrated alongside sacred studies.[10, 12] However, in the yeshiva's tenth year, a sharp internal polemic developed around the demand of parents and Rabbi Avraham Tzukerman to introduce structured high school studies that would enable obtaining a matriculation certificate.[10] Rabbi Tzukerman held that the halakhic obligation of the father to teach his son a craft is implemented in our day through high school education.[10]

Rabbi Neriah initially opposed this in an extreme manner, fearing harm to the totality of Torah study, and even expressed himself to Yisrael Sadan in sharp words: "Hair will grow on the palm of my hand before they study secular subjects in the yeshiva."[10] Ultimately, following heavy social pressure and the establishment of "Midreshet No'am" which offered matriculation studies, Rabbi Neriah was forced to compromise.[10] In the late 1940s high school studies were introduced into the yeshiva at the expense of manual labor, under the direction of Dr. Shmuel Auerbach and with the encouragement of Rabbi Tzukerman, with Dr. Shimshon Novik serving as the first chemistry teacher.[10] This compromise proved historic, as it shaped the "high school yeshiva" model that was replicated in dozens of institutions and enabled the growth of the modern religious-Zionist elite.[10, 11]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Torah Teaching and Thought: Theology of Sovereignty, "Athalta Detquva" and Practical Halakhah

The Torah thought of Rabbi Neriah presented a complex and original theology regarding the State of
Israel and its institutions.[5, 7] In contrast to simplistic messianic conceptions, Rabbi Neriah developed a worldview that regarded the state as a vital instrument for the physical and spiritual survival of the Jewish people, defining it as "athalta de-geulah" (the beginning of redemption).[7] He emphasized that the state is the only place in the world where Jews multiply, speak Hebrew, and develop an independent national identity.[7] His great dream was to raise a young generation that would wage a constant struggle for a "Torah state"—a state in which the army, the economy, the Foreign Ministry, and the Interior Ministry would all be conducted according to the laws of the Torah and halakhah.[5, 7] To this end, an education was required that speaks of army, state, and Zionism from within the beit midrash itself.[5]

Rabbi Neriah was a prolific creator who integrated his spiritual world into the composition of poetry and liturgy.[5] He composed the anthem of the Bnei Akiva movement, "Yad Achim" [2, 5], and edited the text of prayer and thanksgiving for Independence Day, which was accepted almost in its entirety in the synagogues of Religious Zionism.[2, 5] His halakhic oeuvre, as expressed in his numerous Torah essays, was characterized by a systematic view of the challenges of the generation, engaging with diverse subjects [14]:

Principles of the commandments and practical halakhah: clarifications on matters of intention in commandments, "shome'a ke-oneh" (one who hears is as one who responds), laws of minors and commandments, and the blessing over commandments.[14]

Rabbinic authority and halakhic policy: essays on "lo tasur" (you shall not turn aside), the authority of the Great Court, the nature of halakhic adjudication, the place of custom, and the interrelationship between prophecy and halakhah.[14]

Social issues and the value of life: pikuach nefesh (saving a life), the law of the pursuer, saving lives, kiddush Hashem (sanctification of God's name), and the laws of "yehareg ve-al ya'avor" (be killed rather than transgress).[14]

Interpersonal relations and social justice: deception, lashon ha-ra (evil speech), the commandment of rebuke, "love your neighbor as yourself," and the prohibition of "lifnei iver" (placing a stumbling block before the blind).[14]

At the center of his educational doctrine stood a personal, warm, and empowering approach toward the student.[13] He coined the famous saying defining the teacher's mission:

"Every educator must have two loves and three faiths. Love for students and love for the subject, faith in his powers as an educator, faith in the values he seeks to impart to his students, and faith that they will absorb what he invests in them." [1]

He demanded spiritual totality from his students and called upon them to take the yeshiva with them everywhere—to the home, to the street, and to the synagogue.[1] Each morning he would wake his students with a call infused with a Hasidic melody: "Israel, a holy nation, arise for the service of the Creator."[1]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Bridge to Chabad Hasidism and the Lubavitcher Rebbe: Internalizing the Inner Dimension of Torah

Despite being a prominent Religious Zionist leader, Rabbi Neriah maintained throughout his life a direct and deep spiritual and practical connection with Chabad Hasidism and its rebbes.[4] This connection, which began with his clandestine studies in Minsk and was reinforced by the saving of his life by the Rayatz (Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn), permeated deeply into his personal conduct.[4] Rabbi Neriah would pray from the Chabad siddur according to the Ari's version, don tefillin according to Chabad custom, and study daily the daily portion in the Rebbe's sefer Hayom Yom.[4] His wife, Rebbetzin Rachel, testified that the Sefer Tanya lay permanently on his Shabbat table, and his students related that on Rosh Hashanah night he would be immersed in passionate study of the Likutei Torah of the Alter Rebbe (Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi).[4]

The relationship between him and the Lubavitcher Rebbe was characterized by deep mutual respect, exchanges of letters, and extended yechidut (private audiences) in Brooklyn, in which they discussed for long hours educational and halakhic matters.[4] Among the topics raised were the boundaries of modesty in mixed youth movement activity, the obligation to maintain a mechitzah (partition) at public events, and the theological significance of the state.[4]

The Rebbe acted actively to assist Rabbi Neriah; in 5717 (1957), when Rabbi Neriah came to the United States to raise funds for his yeshiva, the Rebbe's secretary, Rabbi Chadakov, telephoned at the Rebbe's instruction to the gaon Rabbi Nissan Telushkin and requested that he employ his influence in Mizrachi circles in the United States to support Rabbi Neriah.[4] The Rebbe even referred students to him who sought to consult with him on matters of combining professional and Torah studies.[4]

His affinity for Chabad found expression also in his influence on his students at the yeshiva, many of whom became in time outright Chabad hasidim, among them Rabbi David Meir Druckman (rabbi of Kiryat Motzkin) and Rabbi Yosef Hartman.[4] On the night following Simchat Torah 5744 (1983), when he received a bottle of liquor from the Rebbe for the yeshiva, Rabbi Neriah drank from it despite his doctors' prohibition at that time, and concluded with emotion that "liquor from the Rebbe cannot harm."[4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Political and Public Activity: Between the Walls of the Knesset and Disillusionment and Ideas of Greater Israel

Alongside his educational work, Rabbi Neriah was a key figure in the public and political arena in the State of Israel, and underwent a tortuous trajectory of parliamentary involvement and disillusionment with it.[4, 5]

His Service in the Knesset and Political Regret

Rabbi Neriah was elected to the Seventh Knesset (1969–1973) as a representative of the National Religious Party (Mafdal).[1, 2, 4] He viewed his Knesset membership as an instrument for fortifying the status of Torah and disseminating the values of religious education at the state level.[3] However, the direct encounter with the party machinery, the cynical compromises, and the narrow interests caused him deep disappointment.[4] Upon retiring from parliamentary life he expressed sharp public regret, saying that his entry into politics was a grave error and that he had "dirtied his hands" in this arena.[4] He emphasized that he infinitely preferred pure and direct educational work over party activism.[5]

The Establishment of the Matzad Movement and the Union of Rabbis

Despite his disappointment with the establishment, Rabbi Neriah did not abandon the public struggle over the character of the state.[3] In 1983, against the background of internal disagreements within Mafdal and an aspiration to lead an uncompromising ideological line on matters of the Land's integrity, he left the party and together with his student Rabbi Chaim Druckman established the Matzad movement (Zionist Religious Party).[4, 12] In the elections to the 11th Knesset he was integrated in a symbolic position (116th place) on the list of the Morasha party.[12]

Rabbi Neriah was a member of the directorate of "The Movement for Greater Israel."[2] In 1993, following the signing of the Oslo Accords and his desire to establish a forceful halakhic and public front against the transfer of territories, he established together with Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli and Rabbi Avraham Shapira the organization "Union of Rabbis for the Land of Israel."[2, 12] This activity emphasized his belief that the Land's integrity and the nation's security are supreme Torah imperatives not subject to temporary political decisions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Creative and Commemorative Enterprise: Mediating the Teachings of the Rayah and Transmitting Them to the Generations

One of Rabbi Neriah's most important enterprises was making accessible the deep and complex doctrine of the Rayah (Rabbi Avraham Yitzchak HaKohen Kook) to the broad public.[3, 5, 15] The teachings of Rav Kook were written in a poetic, kabbalistic, and abstract style, and Rabbi Neriah took upon himself the task of giving them a human, experiential, and accessible face through narrative accounts, ethical discourses, and descriptions of the Rabbi's way of life.[15]

His literary enterprise began with a series of articles he published in the newspaper Hatzofeh, which were subsequently collected into key books published in cooperation with Machon HaTorah VeHa'aretz and the Beit El Library.[15, 16, 17] The books combine original contemplative passages by the Rayah, stories carefully gathered from eyewitnesses and witnesses, and documents from the archive of his father, Rabbi Petachiah Menkin, who was close to the Rayah's circles in Jerusalem.[3, 15]

Parallel to his Torah writing, his educational work was perpetuated through an extensive network of Bnei Akiva yeshivot and ulpanot throughout the Land.[2, 4, 10] His personal archive, including book drafts, political correspondence, and historical letters, is preserved in the National Library and constitutes a valuable research source for the study of the history of Religious Zionism.[3]
Summary and Conclusions

Rabbi Moshe Tzvi Neriah operated as a social and spiritual architect who profoundly influenced the shaping of the character of the modern State of Israel.[2, 3] His figure and work present central conclusions and implications for the development of the religious-Zionist public:

A Unique Cultural Synthesis: Rabbi Neriah demonstrated that it is possible to create a complete religious identity that integrates rigorous halakhic scholarship, Hasidic warmth and experientiality, and uncompromising civic and pioneering commitment.[4, 5, 8] He shattered the old dichotomy between the insular yeshiva world and modern secular pioneering.[5, 10, 12]

Establishment of the Secondary Torah-Education Revolution: The model of Yeshivat Kfar HaRo'eh, despite the polemics that accompanied its founding, became the archetype of religious-Zionist educational institutions.[10] The introduction of secular studies in the spirit of the obligation of "learning a craft" enabled generations of religious youth to integrate into key positions in academia, the economy, the military, and the legal system.[10]

Raising a Generation of Leaders and Pioneers: Rabbi Neriah's students, among them Rabbi Haim Druckman, Rabbi Ya'akov Ariel, Rabbi Dov Lior, and Hanan Porat, became shapers of the path of religious Zionism and its Torah and settlement leaders.[2] Through this, Rabbi Neriah realized his vision of establishing a qualitative and influential human force at the heart of Israeli society.[6]

Rabbi Neriah left behind a theological legacy that views Jewish sovereignty as an immense religious opportunity and a demanding spiritual challenge, while maintaining the principle he coined in his life: "Do not say tomorrow, for tomorrow belongs to God and today is given to you to live and to create".[1, 7]
